Green Hat Boy performance report-back

November 21, 2026 · waveydude · base PS5 9.40 and 13.60

New 13.60 investigation · Earlier Castle Town experiments · Earlier 9.40 report-back

Findings from the later 13.60 runs

Depth feedback reduced measured GPU work. Two 13.60 pairs cut main 1080p render-target work from roughly 30 to 8 ms/frame. That is the clearest evidence for the mechanism. Across five 9.40 pairs, median FPS moved 11.26 → 12.67 and the median worst frame 132 → 117 ms. Pair 2 lost 0.79 FPS and pair 4 moved only +0.36 FPS. Both had substantially worse worst frames. Everything below investigates the Town slowdown that remains with the depth fix enabled.

Repeated decompression is real. In one traced Town pass, 2,275 of 2,284 decompressions fetched a chunk that was still in the same packed generation. Only nine were the first tracked read and zero reread a slot after its generation changed. Allocation-refusal recovery originally packed 1,306 of those chunks' read events, pressure scans 936, ordinary cold scans 38, and graphics reclaim 4. These counts are reads, including repeat reads, rather than unique chunks.

Ledger switch names. Patch 0564 is EDEN_UP_UBO_BIND_TRIM. Patch 1004 is EDEN_UP_BACKX. Patch 0750 is EDEN_UP_EXACT_EMPTY_SUBMITS. The depth fix is EDEN_UP_DEPTH_FEEDBACK_RECHECK. The shared screenshot guard is EDEN_UP_SCREENSHOT_DROP_ON_OOM.

Upscalers. The earlier 13.60 entrance and fountain replays used Bilinear. The later shared 13.60 Town replays in this section used AMD FSR. Both used handheld 1× at 1080p/60 Hz.

What happened in the 11.72 FPS run

The 14.53 FPS and 11.72 FPS replays used the same existing selection order. Neither had older candidates for the experimental order to promote. Their shader store, route contents, starting save and executable matched. In the scored stretch the faster replay recorded 3,022 repeat unpacks, including 1,650 total unpacks from refusal-packed slots. The slower replay recorded 5,372 repeat unpacks and 4,237 total refusal-source unpacks.

During the sampled intervals between +10 and +15 s after the archive request, the repeats were close, 764 versus 771. Between +15 and +19 s the counts were 1,246 versus 1,941. In those same intervals, unpacks from refusal-packed slots rose 570 → 1,375 despite the slower run starting Town only slightly later in the app. This is where the slower run's unpack workload first visibly pulls away. Counts use the first and last complete counter snapshots in each bin.

The slow run also had an additional 2 MiB allocation refusal at +20.57 s, after the divergence had already started. The allocator logged a largest free piece of 1 MiB before a drain. Recovery packed 64 guest-memory chunks, took 171 ms, and reported about 65 MiB returned. The graphics allocation succeeded on retry. The same trace shows a 250.6 ms worst presentation frame somewhere in that run's scored windows. There is no exact frame-level match between that worst frame and the refusal. The early recovery passes already differed in which chunks they selected even when the ordering rule was identical. The available runs do not identify the specific recovery pass that originally packed each later read, or why the two runs selected different individual chunks. Testing stopped before a per-pass provenance probe ran.

How the investigation reached guest-memory decompression

Check on 13.60 Measured result Status
Command reader and recorder One 10.1 s Town interval logged 5,189 ms waiting for the recorder, 172 ms in direct list-copy waits, and 122 ms in direct recorder GPU wait. These are distinct scopes. Locator for further work.
Recorder patch 1004 Checked 53,079 skipped gathers and 1,505,777 skipped inline locks, with 20 observed concurrent-write races and zero missed updates. Timed OFF 13.54, ON 14.32, repeat OFF 14.24 FPS. Correctness coverage for this route. The controls nearly bracketed the apparent gain.
Slow recorder frames 112 sampled slow frames. Stage binding was the largest named operation at a 27.8 ms median. A lighter split attributed 89.9% of sampled binding time to uniforms and 10.1% to storage. Texture binds had no sampled calls. Timing instrumentation only.
Existing uniform shortcut 0564 OFF controls 14.23 and 12.60 FPS, ON 16.02 and 14.25 FPS. Mean per sampled binding 3.344 and 4.320 µs OFF, 2.243 and 3.316 µs ON. A separate verifier checked 18.39M memory-state decisions and 2.03M bank lookups, with zero differences. Reduces repeated checks. Larger FPS gain did not repeat.
Where the slow uniform batches appeared The two identical ON replays had 3 of 49 versus 25 of 43 sampled batch means above 4 µs in the first ten scored seconds. A 210 ms staging allocation nested inside a 211 ms texture upload ended before the recurring slow binding batches. Entrance hitch and later slow batches are distinct observations.
Inside buffer synchronization A coverage-checked probe accounted for all 8,479 sampled synchronization calls in 79 batches. Existing memoization avoided scans in 6,972 calls. Actual uploads explained 98.5% of the extra synchronization time in slow batches. Clean scans were a small part of this slowdown.
Inside uploads Two runs measured 14.61 and 15.25 FPS, with 118.9 and 104.8 ms worst frames. Reading guest data into staging explained 98.1% and 98.6% of the slower batches' extra upload time. Getting staging space and recording the GPU copy were much smaller in these samples.
Inside guest reads Slow batches had 28 LZ4 unpacks, with zero file reads, restored slots, or scratch-cache hits. Actual LZ4 time explained about 90% of the guest-read increase, around 0.57 ms per unpack. The diagnostic scored 13.88 FPS, with a 348.7 ms worst frame whose individual cause was not isolated. Direct timing of unpack work serving sampled uniform reads.

The first page-scan attempt returned zero inner counts because the build did not reliably reach the instrumented Vulkan implementation. That split is unavailable. The rebuilt probe compiled both Vulkan callers and checked that the internal path counts matched the caller totals before scoring. Probe timings explain work within the same capture and should remain separate from low-overhead FPS comparisons.

Two follow-up fixes tested

13.60 comparison OFF ON What the trace verified
4 MiB extra unpack cache 13.55 FPS / 119.8 ms worst 13.27 FPS / 126.2 ms worst ON avoided 367 unpacks through real cache hits. It still logged 4,363 compressed misses versus 2,125 OFF. One matched pair, with different full-window alignment and memory workloads. Cache is off outside the test.
Older-first refusal order, first pair 14.90 FPS / 110.2 ms worst 13.99 FPS / 114.3 ms worst OFF returned the requested bytes in 5/5 passes, ON in 5/6. The short ON pass returned 50.64 of 64 MiB and had no older candidate to prioritize. Both routes completed.
Older-first refusal order, reverse pair 11.72 FPS / 250.6 ms worst 14.53 FPS / 115.0 ms worst OFF 7/7, ON 6/6 recovery passes returned the requested bytes. Neither run had older candidates, so their sorting behavior was identical regardless of the switch.

The expanded cache-off trace saw 2,125 GPU-reader compressed misses. Metadata-only replays of the lookup history put 230 / 454 / 1,240 of these chunks within the last 2 / 4 / 8 distinct lookups. The actual test kept just one extra 2 MiB slot for each of two GPU readers. A hit requires the original slot lock and the same range, slot, packed location, packed size, and generation. The larger history sizes were measured as metadata only.

The older-first candidate is default-off. Only two of 24 allocation recoveries across its four runs had older candidates, with one opportunity while enabled. It changes only the order within the existing cold candidates and retains the fallback, budget, and original pressure scanner. The tests give no repeatable FPS or hitch improvement attributable to the switch.

Reproducing the new numbers

  • Base PS5 13.60, matched per experiment. Handheld 1×, AMD FSR, 1080p output and the existing 81,002 warm pipelines in prep_8ba969cb. The 9.40 five-pair set used 81,025 pipelines in its own verified warm store. Comparison scores are within each firmware build and test family.
  • The scripted Town replay starts from the same disposable fixture. Both original save sets verified after completed runs. The 13.60 Town profile stayed selected between runs, with the original play configuration backed up separately. A transfer interruption during the first cache-ON staging attempt was recovered and verified before the successful retry. That aborted staging attempt has no FPS.
  • The timing tables use complete five-second presentation windows in the +19 to +35 s Castle Town interval. Windows start at slightly different offsets and can contain different amounts of walking and standing. The two types of diagnostics have overhead. Use the raw windows and matched settings when comparing arms.
  • The 9.40 live-play capture with depth recheck and exact empty-submits both enabled measured 14.48 and 15.91 FPS in its two complete Town windows. Worst frames were 230.1 and 115.4 ms. This is a live-play observation alongside the scripted measurements.

Earlier Castle Town experiments

The depth-feedback fix took median Castle Town FPS from 11.26 to 12.67 (+12.5%) across five matched pairs on 9.40. The median worst frame dropped from 132 to 117 ms. Link reached the final street checkpoint sooner in four of five pairs. The big entrance hitch and a sustained 15 FPS are still open.

The fix checks whether the current draw reads the active depth image. Draws with a real overlap still get the required barrier. The previous optimization could reuse a decision across draws that bind different views. A separate 9.40 diagnostic pair matched each measured long wait to its exact emulated fence signal. The median time before the signal fell by 10.16 ms with the fix on. Once the signal arrived, the game resumed in about 0.015 ms in both arms. The median delay from recording a sampled submission to the Vulkan worker picking it up was about 0.036 ms. Those timings put the bottleneck before the signal, with little time spent waking the game or handing commands to Vulkan.

With detailed pass timing off, a same-build 13.60 comparison went 12.57 → 14.40 FPS and 62.2 → 53.1 ms mean fence wait. The worst frame was similar at 115.2 → 116.1 ms. The 13.60 GPU measurements describe one part of that work and are kept separate from the 9.40 FPS benchmark.

A shorter wait for command reads on 9.40

Some reads wait for the command recorder to drain all queued work. Lichii’s #1028 option waits for queued commands that may write the memory being read and still uses the full read path when needed. A separate verifier checked about 8,900 eligible reads in one Town window against the original method and logged zero mismatches. I kept depth recheck enabled for both performance arms.

Pair Targeted wait off → on Town FPS off → on Worst frame off → on Banner to final checkpoint off → on

2, ON first 319.4 → 156.1 ms/s 12.79 → 14.98 356.0 → 114.4 ms 14.86 → 13.32 s

The narrower path reduced measured time per miss from 0.255 to 0.168 ms in pair 1 and from 0.312 to 0.134 ms in pair 2. Matching the number of nearby FPS windows gave 13.67 off and 11.98 on in pair 1. Pair 2 already used two windows in both arms. The targeted wait consistently fell. FPS, worst frame and checkpoint time reversed direction across pairs, leaving a repeatable gameplay gain unverified.

What still happens at the gate

A single graphics frame about 11 seconds after the archive request uploaded roughly 808 MiB of images plus 362 MiB of buffers. In one traced comparison, the largest individual image upload in that frame was 32.2 MiB. The later slow 2 MiB scratch allocations were a separate part of the load.

On 9.40, enabling one CPU helper for large texture conversions reduced measured image upload work in the first big frame from 266.5 → 245.5 ms at the same 807.7 MiB and 761 uploads. The worst displayed entrance frame got longer, from 603.5 → 721.4 ms. A return to the control recorded 664.1 ms at the entrance and 275.8 ms of image upload work. The helper reduced the timed upload work in that burst. The displayed freeze remained the bigger problem.

On 13.60, both drain-to-pool arms reached the same Town scene and stopped inside the market gateway. Both had 161 presented frames over closely aligned windows roughly +24 to +34 seconds after the archive request.

All eight ideas

# Idea What the tests established
1 Use earlier traces to find what can go A manually derived profile for the Field-to-Town transition improved the typical moving run. A general predictor remains open.
2 Reserve and reuse graphics memory A small Town scratch reserve prevented some slow allocations. The fountain counts varied, and a general startup reserve remains unproven.
3 Protect essential work under pressure The optional screenshot-drop path passed host checks. The live check encountered no eligible allocation failure. Trinity found four crash stacks in the test’s own screenshot read, supporting the failure mechanism. The guard still needs a hardware case that exercises it.
4 Evict old texture copies and rebuild later The #1 experiment removed two copies totaling 117.07 MiB through the measured Town segment. The return trip and rebuild cost still need measurement.
5 Track allocations by area Tracking last use around this entrance located cold Field textures. Automatic tagging and cleanup by area remain open.
6 Clean up during loading Two early packing runs packed about 259–260 MiB in 558–621 ms. The largest free block stayed flat during packing. Refusal counts were 14 in the reference and 4 in both packing runs, with different starting headroom. A same-build one-switch comparison is the follow-up.
7 Reduce the cost of large render targets The existing fast clear avoided a 288 MiB temporary upload at each of two measured loads. The 297 MiB resident depth image remained. Format and dimension changes still need their own test.
8 Measure where graphics memory goes The traces separated old resident textures, the first upload burst, and later scratch stalls. A fully correlated allocation and GPU-completion lifetime trace remains open.

Credit to Trinity for the symbolized screenshot stacks. Discord report

Earlier 9.40 report-back

waveydude · Base PS5 · Firmware 9.40

I cleared the earlier dungeon with both DualSense mic modes working, then cleared the later dungeon in Docked with drain-to-pool on. The the later dungeon video also caught memory getting critical after the clear, back at Lake Hylia. A separate Docked run crashed in Kakariko with the same load switches on. I’ve got a better picture now of where the memory fix helps and where it runs out of room.

1. Flash counter and the team’s results

GBB tested my patch 1211 on the shared alpha, four warm Field starts OFF and four ON, using the same executable. Field walking was 14.41 vs. 14.42 FPS, the heavy section was 14.65 vs. 14.70 FPS, and 4/4 made it through the load on each side. Worst frame was 391 vs. 452 ms, which leaned higher with the counter on and was within his allowance for variation. The result was no measurable cost in that batch. PR #29 is merged.

My own exact T186 port passed the host detector tests and PS5 package checks. The 9.40 the earlier dungeon play build reported 332 brightness-change candidates in 81,254 sampled frames, with zero busy-slot skips. The biggest burst was 42 in 245 samples. That needs footage to tell whether it was a real glitch or normal effects. The gate should use the totals from completed summaries, require positive frame coverage, and leave picture results unavailable when the detector or video can’t measure them.

GBB also took the guest swapper out of the control. All three starts crashed on the exit from the field with about 1 MiB free. He set up a 24-start batch to find which parts of the swapper matter. Trinity’s Docked T191 batch had 0/7 crashes with the two load switches and saw the long memory waits return when park wait was added. That is why I’m testing those settings separately on 9.40.

Sources: GBB’s Appendix H · Flash-counter PR #29 · Trinity’s Docked evidence.

2. the earlier dungeon and the mic fix

I beat the boss without a crash after checking both Humming and Instruments in the same session. Humming had been feeding the pitch detector a silent stream. My Zelda v2.0.0 test IPS routes the real DualSense audio to that detector and leaves Instruments using its original stream order. Both worked in the game on 9.40. The mic fix has yet to be verified on 13.60.

The log covers 42:21 since launch, with about 32.6 presentation FPS overall. The 30 seconds leading up to my reported clear averaged 34.5 FPS, with zero frames over 100 ms in those six windows. The worst frame over the full capture was 704 ms, early in the session. There were no logged OOM events, and the driver’s smallest sampled free block was 846 MiB. There was no matching video, so the exact boss clear frame and the flash candidates stay unclassified.

Mic write-up · the earlier dungeon chart and notes.

Kakariko still crashed with the setting working, including a pass that returned 650 MiB.

4. What the earlier Docked runs add

The archived 9.40 runs used the same play executable and reused the same shader-store name, prep_8ba969cb. They started from different saves and took different routes. The older run with drain-to-pool off had 33 MiB as its lowest driver sample by 70 minutes, hit 0 MiB around 77:15, and crashed after 2:10:39. Two shorter Docked runs with it off reached 0 MiB sooner, one while making it through town. I completed the later dungeon before memory pressure became critical at Lake Hylia. Both long runs showed a largest free block of 0 MiB around 76–77 minutes, and the different routes prevent a direct runtime comparison.

In a separate W-39 Kakariko check, the two Handheld starts bottomed out at 79–81 MiB and the two Docked starts at 2–3 MiB. Every start reached Kakariko. Turning drain-to-pool on shortened the worst frame in the Docked pair from 538 to 494 ms. The Handheld pair moved from 489 to 568 ms. Each comparison is one pair on that route, and the final positions in Handheld differed.

The two crash signatures matter. The earlier long-run crash reported an invalid access on a game CPU thread after a nearly 10-second memory wait reclaimed nothing. The later Kakariko crash reported an invalid access on GPUBack. Both occurred under heavy memory pressure, and the failed operations may differ. The Kakariko crash is also separate from the PS5 Pro tester’s Castle Town fountain report in issue #28.

5. Death Mountain and Lakeside findings

  • Keeping the 171 MiB buffer around longer helped in all three measured pairs. Rebuilds fell from 7 to 3–4, and the worst frame fell by 53–68 ms. All six scored runs reached Kakariko. The low memory reading improved in two of the three pairs. There was still roughly a half-second hitch.
  • The load and the stutter need separate numbers. The three usable video checks showed 17.6–18.5 seconds of black loading. About 20.5 FPS was typical during the scored downhill movement. A trace found 643 ms of graphics command-reader waits on a slow frame, mostly 278 ms on fresh DMA reads, 244 ms waiting for command-list writers, and 99 ms checking graphics signals.
  • Shortening the DMA wait passed a correctness check on this route. All 28,012 checked reads matched the fully drained read byte for byte. The next ON run missed Continue and stayed at the title menu, so it supplies no performance result. The replacement route uses a visible Continue check and still needs hardware qualification.
  • Zero-depth clear saved real staging memory. Two qualifying 12,288 × 12,288 depth uploads were cleared in place, avoiding 288 MiB of temporary staging each. The checks took 5.1 and 4.8 ms. The old manual load showed a 728 ms frame versus 618 ms in one scripted run with the new build. The different run methods leave the size of the speedup open.
  • Lakeside Laboratory exposed a capture failure. The long route ended after a refused 8,294,400-byte GPU transfer buffer allocation, with earlier memory warnings already present. That size matches a screenshot readback buffer. The exact caller is inferred. The recovery code passed host fault-injection checks for failed screenshot image and download-buffer allocations. It still needs validation at the original crash spot.

6. Current state and the next useful Docked check
